Record date: 2129-11-28
South Elizabeth Seychelles Hospital INTERNAL MEDICINE DEPARTMENT Location: 4923 Olivia Parkway Suite 217, Lake Jennabury
PATIENT: Lysander Fairfax Phone: 28451903 email:bradleymorgan@example.org DATE OF BIRTH: 1947-05-12 AGE: 80 years
FOLLOW-UP DATE: 11/28/29 FOLLOWED BY: Dr. Emily Carter
CHIEF COMPLAINT
Worsening shortness of breath, persistent productive cough, and increased fatigue.
HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Mr. Lysander Fairfax returns for a follow-up visit after one week of continued treatment with oral Doxycycline and Prednisone for his chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) exacerbation. He reports that his cough remains productive with yellow sputum, which has not improved since his last visit. He describes his shortness of breath as worsening, particularly with minimal exertion, and notes that he experiences increased chest tightness. Fatigue has significantly impacted his ability to perform daily tasks, and he states that he feels more exhausted than before. He denies any fever or chills but reports occasional night sweats.
Mr. Fairfax has been compliant with his medication regimen but notes that he has had to increase the frequency of his nebulized albuterol to every 4 hours due to persistent wheezing and shortness of breath.
REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
General - + increased fatigue, - weight loss, - fever, - chills, + night sweats. Pulmonary - + persistent productive cough with yellow sputum, + increased wheezing, - hemoptysis. Cardiac - no chest pain, - orthopnea, - paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea. Gastrointestinal - no nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea. Musculoskeletal - no joint pain. Neurological - no dizziness or headaches.
PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vital Signs: - Blood Pressure: 130/76 mmHg - Heart Rate: 80 bpm - Respiratory Rate: 30 breaths/min - Oxygen Saturation: 85% on room air.
General: The patient appears fatigued and in moderate respiratory distress.
HEENT: No nasal flaring; oropharynx clear, no signs of dehydration.
Lungs: Significant wheezing on auscultation; decreased breath sounds bilaterally; prolonged expiration with audible rhonchi and increased use of accessory muscles.
Cardiac: Regular rate and rhythm, no murmurs or gallops; peripheral pulses intact and symmetric.
Extremities: No edema; no tenderness on palpation.
ASSESSMENT
1. Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) exacerbation with persistent symptoms despite current treatment; worsening cough, shortness of breath, and fatigue warrant reevaluation of therapeutic approach. 2. Possible underlying bacterial infection contributing to respiratory symptoms, given the persistence of yellow sputum. 3. Congestive heart failure stable; no signs of fluid overload or exacerbation.
PLAN
1. Obtain a sputum culture and sensitivity to identify any potential bacterial pathogens and adjust antibiotic therapy accordingly. 2. Initiate oral Azithromycin 500 mg daily for 5 days to cover atypical pathogens, given the lack of improvement on Doxycycline. 3. Continue oral Prednisone 20 mg daily for one more week to manage inflammation associated with COPD exacerbation. 4. Increase the dose of Salmeterol to 100 mcg twice daily and Tiotropium to maintain bronchodilation; consider adding a systemic bronchodilator if symptoms do not improve. 5. Recommend the use of a corticosteroid inhaler (Fluticasone/Salmeterol) to help manage inflammation and improve respiratory function. 6. Encourage Mr. Fairfax to continue light physical activity as tolerated and to utilize his nebulizer as needed for symptom relief. 7. Schedule a follow-up appointment in one week to reassess respiratory status, culture results, and overall symptomatology. If no improvement is noted, consider referral to a pulmonologist for further evaluation, including potential imaging studies or pulmonary function tests.
DISPOSITION
Mr. Fairfax was discharged home with a revised medication regimen that includes Azithromycin, continued Prednisone, and adjustments to his inhaled medications. He was educated on the importance of adhering to the new treatment plan and instructed to closely monitor his symptoms. A follow-up appointment has been scheduled for one week from today to evaluate the effectiveness of the ongoing treatment and to make necessary adjustments based on his clinical progress.
